messages.body_plain:
First post here- thanks in advance for your help.  This is potentially both a math question and an R question.

I have timeseries data where the data were collected at a certain interval (e.g. at 22hz).  I need to convert these to a new timeseries that has a less frequent sampling interval (e.g at 12hz). I haven't found a specific function that can do this, so it seems like I'll need to do this in two steps- 1) use a function like a spline  on the original data to approximate the original time series, 2) apply a vector of new sampling times to the spline.

Can anyone weigh in on pros/cons of different spline functions (or point me to a quick discussion that would be intelligible for someone who is maybe not super mathy)? It seems like there are a lot of them, and I'm not really sure how best to choose.

Thanks!
Alan

messages.subject: Re: Gaussian Process Models and map2stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dena,

First: Richard's package is a really convenient way to quickly implement models from R to Stan, but it is quite limited and not too difficult to break.  For more complex models such as yours, it might be well worth the investment to learn to code a Stan model directly. The Stan development team has great packages to use with R (rstan and shinystan), as well as an active forum to get help. Coding the model directly opens up a lot more flexibility and robustness.

Second: While Stan is fast, it can struggle with GP models with lots of observations. For reference, a GP model with reasonable complexity and 1600 observations took several hours to fit running in parallel on 8 cores.  A much faster alternative is Aki's GPstuff. There is an interface so you can use it straight from R.

Assuming you want to continue to use Richard's package:

- Replace the Poisson distribution with one that makes sense for your data (e.g. - normal). Make sure you add code for the additional required parameters (e.g. - sigma).
- I believe the GPL2 function uses a distance matrix as input. You can calculate this in R to hand to map2stan, but make sure to convert to a matrix from the default output for dist(). Stan does not like the vector representation of matrices.
- If you have multiple observations from the same location, the GPL2 should account for this automatically with the jitter included in the L2 function. (Observations with the same distance have a little noise added to avoid perfect correlations.) I believe the last variable in the GPL2 function is the jitter amount (not 100% sure without looking it up).

Hope that helps,

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Downsampling time series
messages.body_plain:
We run into this quite a bit with stream logger data and timelapse photo data. I'm not familiar with working in hz, but concept should work.

One approach is to set an interval and then round your times to that interval, then aggregate. Example below rounds to nearest 15 minutes.

## weird random data set, requires "lubridate" package
require(lubridate)
times<-seq(ymd_hms("2015-01-01 01:03:15"), ymd_hms("2015-01-02 23:14:12"),by = hms("0:33:22"))

## Round to nearest 15 min:
interval <- 15 # set to 15 minutes
timesround <- as.POSIXct(round(as.double(times)/(interval*60))*(interval*60),origin=(as.POSIXct(tz="GMT",'1970-01-01')))

df<-data.frame("time"=time, "timeround"=timeround, "data"=rnorm(7558,2,1))

## Now use dplyr to aggregate
df2 <- df %>%
  mutate("year"=year(timeround),
         "month"=month(timeround),
         "yday"=yday(timeround),
         "hour"=hour(timeround),
         "minute"=minute(timeround)) %>%
  group_by(year, month, yday, hour, minute)%>%
  summarize("min15.avg"=mean(data)) %>%
  mutate("datetime"=ymd_hms(strptime(paste0(year,"-", month,"-", yday, " ",
                                            hour,":", minute, ":00"),format = "%Y-%m-%j %H:%M:%S"))) %T>%
  with(plot(datetime, min15.avg, col="blue")) %>%
  as.data.frame()

## I've also seen a modulo approach i.e.,
## use dplyr and use numeric column to mutate your time by a given interval

mutate(df, "min3" = paste0(minute(time) - minute(time)%%3, "m"))

Hope this helps,
Adios,
Ryan

Workshop announcement: Pydoit for workflow automation - local + remote

Who: Camille Scott (Lead Instructor)
When: January 20, 2016
Times: 9 am-12:15 pm
Where: TBD (UC Davis campus)

Descriptions:

Pydoit is a task management and automation tool, similar to ‘make’ (comparison: http://swcarpentry.github.io/bc/intermediate/doit/make-vs-doit.html). Tasks are defined individually and executed in order according to dependencies, via a directed acyclic graph. The basic building blocks of a pydoit workflow are tasks, which encode the work we would like to get done. Here is an extremely simple task:

def task_hello_world():
   return {'actions': ['echo "hello world!" > hello.txt’ ],
               'targets': ['hello.txt’]}

The task is a python function prefixed with task, which returns a dictionary containing some predefined entries. The actions entry is a list of the actual commands we'd like to run, in this case, a single shell command. The targets entry is a list of the files output by this task.  Of course, hello world doesn't really do anything for us. Throughout this lesson, we're going to build a pipeline which downloads some data, plots it with matplotlib, generates a markup file with the chart, and outputs a final compiled document -- in other words, a barebones version of a publication pipeline.

This workshop will be broadcast to several other locations via Google Hangouts, but will be taught locally at UC Davis.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zach,

I think Vince is right in that sed or perl is the traditional/efficient way to parse large amounts sequence data.

If you are set on R, grep and regex should be able get you where you need to go (depending on the size of the task).

Its not clear from the question what exactly the data.frame you want looks like (eg what are the rows and what are the columns?).
 Assuming you want something like column1 = id and column 2 = sequence, heres how I would do it:

# test.txt is the text file containing data. This loads it as a vector with one line of data per 'slot'.
d <- readLines <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base/readLines>('test.txt')
head <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/utils/head>(d)

# identify all characters between an '@' or '+' at the beginning of a line and the sequence 'read_id=';replace with either + or @
d <- gsub <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base/gsub>( pattern = '(^@|^[+]).*?read_id=', replacement = '\\1', x = d )

# remove the barcode tag
d <- gsub <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base/gsub>( pattern = 'barcode=CGGCATAT', replacement = '', x = d)

# reform into a data.frame
ids <- grep <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base/grep>('(^@|^[+])', d) #indices of 'ids'
my.df <- data.frame <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base/data.frame> ( id = d[ids], sequence <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base/sequence> = d[-ids])
head <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/utils/head>(my.df)

Created by Pretty R at inside-R.org <http://www.inside-r.org/pretty-r>
Hope this helps --

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zach,

> 1) It printed the (correct) output in the terminal, but did not alter the file itself or produce a new output file.

Yes, this is expected. You never want to modify data in place. You should treat data as read-only, always. Why? What if an unexpected error occurred and it left your files destroyed?

The right way to handle this is to redirect the standard output of sed to a file with >. For example:

$ sed 's/\([@\\+]\).*read_id=\([^\s]*\) .*$/\1\2/' test.fq > new_file.fq

> 2) I have a directory with multiple FASTQ files, named 81.fastq, 82. fastq, etc. I need to perform this function on every file in the directory. What's the best way to do this, instead of running the same function on each file individually?

I would recommend you use find + xargs. It should take less than ten minutes to do this using these tools (learning them is a great investment, especially in bioinformatics), but I must admit, trying to explain how they work over email is going to be tricky. You can find a reference here: http://www.linuxplanet.com/linuxplanet/tutorials/6522/1 or my book <http://shop.oreilly.com/product/0636920030157.do> covers this in depth too. You will need to wrap the sed command in a simple bash script too, as you need the file name to be used in the output file too, and you need to use redirects.

Vince

messages.body_plain:
Hey Zach,

It seems like most of what you're wanting to do is probably better done in Bash using tools like sed instead of R (although as Steve indicated, there are some R functions that might get you equivalent results). To add to what Vince just said, I would probably accomplish this task using a for loop in a Bash script something like so (although this may not be the most elegant or fastest solution):

#!/bin/bash
set -eu

for file in 1 2 3

do

# Define input file and output file names
InputFile="Input"$file".fq"

OutputFile="Output"$file".fq"

# Perform your sed operations
sed 's/\([@\\+]\).*read_id=\([^\s]*\) .*$/\1\2/' $InputFile > $OutputFile

done

So assuming you execute this script from a directory containing the files "Input1.fq", "Input2.fq", and "Input3.fq", you would get back "Output1.fq", "Output2.fq", and "Output3.fq" which would have been modified using that sed command. You can of course modify the script according to the file names/file paths you actually have and the output files you want.

Hope that helps!
Evan

messages.body_plain:
I think the only issue is that:

for file in 1 2 3

is not very robust (what if you forget to type out a number?) and not dynamic (what if you add a new file and forget to change your script accordingly?). You can use find to propagate this list automatically, as long as you use a clear naming scheme. This is how I'd tackle it.

$ mkdir fastq_files output
$ cd fastq_files
$ touch {1..10}.fq # make test data
$ cd ..

Then save this (below) to process.sh and chmod u+x it:

#!/bin/bash
set -e
set -u
set -o pipefail

FILEKEY=$(basename $1 .fq) # strip data directory and extension

echo "processing file $FILEKEY"
sed 's/\([@\\+]\).*read_id=\([^\s]*\) .*$/\1\2/' fastq_files/${FILEKEY}.fq > output/${FILEKEY}_processed.fq

for testing, I also threw in my test.fq from earlier into fastq_files.

Then do:

$ find fastq_files -name "*.fq"
fastq_files/1.fq
fastq_files/10.fq
fastq_files/2.fq
fastq_files/3.fq
fastq_files/4.fq
fastq_files/5.fq
fastq_files/6.fq
fastq_files/7.fq
fastq_files/8.fq
fastq_files/9.fq
fastq_files/test.fq

Note how we just use extension to match FASTQ files. You may wish to be less permissive, depending on your project structure, etc. Verify that these are indeed the same files you want to process.

Then we just pipe these names into xargs, which takes a single name (with the -n 1 option) and passes it to process.sh, with:

$ find fastq_files -name "*.fq" | xargs -n 1 ./process.sh

All output is saved with the suffix _processed.fq. The numbered FASTQ files were empty, so no results, but test_processed.fq verifies everything looks like it's working. This should be fast enough, but if you need to run it in parallel, you can use -P 10 or something with xargs. Just beware spawning 10 subprocesses may make you unpopular on shared resources, depending on the etiquette and resources there and so forth.

Vince

PS: If you really feel like digging into Unix hackery, GNU parallel has some nice options that can prevent the need for a bash wrapper, but it's a bit tricky.

>From my experience, Rstudio embeds everything into those encoded scripts that it needs to render the page (that it is aware of). I sometimes use jquery in some reports I make and I have to add a line in the top of my file. Rstudio incorporates this into the output. The problem with this approach is that if you're running a webpage, your scripts might be reused and you should store them in a single place, or have your user go fetch them from the interwebs. Yihui told me a while ago that bootstrap stylings and mathjax are embedded automagically in HTML Rmd outputs through Rstudio. You can turn this off in the YAML header (highlighted in pink) and it will save significant size of the final file. output: html_document: mathjax: null theme: null highlight: null pandoc_args: [ "+RTS", "-K64m", "-RTS" ] It looks like everything is fine, but you're missing a required visualization library for the visNetwork output in your non-Rstudio output. If you want to embed that, you need to know what it needs I guess. I can't seem to find anything specific enough to your issue though. Doing multiple t-tests on the same data set is usually frowned upon. Is there some reason why you want to compare each of the time points to zero and not do a linear model using all the time points? That would look like this:

m1 = glm(meas ~ time, data = dfs)
summary(m1)

# If you want all the comparisons, you can always just do an ANOVA and a post-hoc to get the comparisons of each time step
# to zero (and to each of the other time steps). This would be more appropriate than a t-test for each time point.
dfs$time2 = as.factor(dfs$time)
m2 = aov(meas ~ time2, data = dfs)
summary(m2)
TukeyHSD(m2)

# if you want it in a table, the plyr package may be your friend
library(plyr)
dfs2 = ddply(dfs, .(Genes, time), summarize, mmeas = mean(meas))

That should give you a new data frame with the mean of the measurement for each time point. Hope that helps!

Hi Sharon,

The reason to model all genes simultaneously is to avoid finding significance in what is really just noise. Simply, the more things you measure the greater likelihood some will look significant when they are not. The means comparison methods are calibrated to control this compounding error rate, but this goes out the window when you are running hundreds or thousands of models. Without knowing your data better, I would say that different responses do not necessarily ensure independence.

My little bit of code just showed how to run the times as a category. Looking a bit more carefully at your data, it appears you have some additional structure in your data (reps). To get a functional model for this is a bit more involved if your times are grouped.

There are some pretty slick packages for modeling genomic data that enforce some level of sparsity (thereby control error rates). I don't do genomic work, so can cannot name any off hand, but I know this is the type of work that Dr. Dan Runcie does. I am sure there are some people on this list that also could help with this.

Matt
